stem: After handling a patient’s soiled linen, a nurse removes gloves and prepares to adjust a clean vascular dressing. What is needed before the next task?

options.label: A
options.text: Perform hand hygiene before the clean task.

options.label: B
options.text: Put on new gloves without cleaning the hands.

options.label: C
options.text: Clean the hands only after both tasks are finished.

options.label: D
options.text: Wipe the hands on a clean disposable towel.

answerText: Perform hand hygiene before the clean task.
rationale: Glove removal can contaminate the hands. Hand hygiene is needed before a clean or aseptic task.

misconceptions.B: A new pair of gloves does not clean the hands.
misconceptions.C: Delayed hand hygiene permits transfer of organisms.
misconceptions.D: A dry towel is not an effective hand-hygiene method.

pearl: Clean hands are required between contaminated and clean care.
trap: Mistaking gloves for hand hygiene.

stem: A stable adult is prescribed 600 mL of intravenous fluid over 5 hours. What is the correct pump rate in mL/hour?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: 240 mL/hour.

options.label: C
options.text: 12 mL/hour.

options.label: D
options.text: 120 mL/hour.

answerText: 120 mL/hour.
rationale: Divide the prescribed volume by the time in hours. The result is 120 mL/hour.

misconceptions.A: This halves the required rate.
misconceptions.B: This doubles the required rate.
misconceptions.C: This introduces a tenfold error.

pearl: For mL/hour, divide the volume by the duration in hours.
trap: Changing the unit without checking the calculation.

stem: During the first minutes of a red-cell transfusion, a patient develops rigors and new flank pain. Which action comes first?

stem: An adult working outside is agitated and unable to follow commands after heavy exertion. Core temperature is 40.4°C. Help is on the way. Which action is most appropriate?

misconceptions.D: Antipyretics do not treat heat accumulation from exertion.

stem: An adult choosing to fast reports hunger, sweating, and palpitations. Glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. The patient is alert and can swallow. What should the nurse prioritize?

options.label: A
options.text: Break the fast, take 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, and recheck glucose after 15 minutes.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue fasting and recheck glucose at sunset.

options.label: C
options.text: Take extra rapid-acting insulin and rest.

options.label: D
options.text: Eat only a high-fat snack and recheck the next morning.

answerText: Break the fast, take 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, and recheck glucose after 15 minutes.
rationale: The alert adult can swallow safely and needs prompt oral treatment of hypoglycaemia, even during a chosen fast. Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck after 15 minutes; repeat treatment if glucose remains below 3.9 mmol/L, and seek urgent help if recovery fails or swallowing becomes unsafe.

misconceptions.B: Waiting allows hypoglycaemia to worsen.
misconceptions.C: Additional insulin can lower glucose further.
misconceptions.D: Fat slows absorption and overnight delay is unsafe.

pearl: Treat low glucose promptly even during a chosen fast.
trap: Delaying necessary treatment to preserve the fast.

stem: An adult with DKA is being prepared for intravenous insulin. The latest potassium is 2.8 mmol/L. Which response is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Escalate the low potassium and arrange replacement before starting insulin.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Ignore potassium until the glucose concentration falls.

options.label: D
options.text: Give routine bicarbonate instead of reporting the potassium.

answerText: Escalate the low potassium and arrange replacement before starting insulin.
rationale: Insulin shifts potassium into cells and can worsen dangerous hypokalaemia. Current adult DKA guidance delays insulin when potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L while replacement is arranged.

misconceptions.B: An intracellular shift would worsen the existing deficit.
misconceptions.C: Arrhythmias can occur before glucose has normalized.
misconceptions.D: Bicarbonate is not a substitute for appropriate potassium management.

pearl: A low potassium level can change the order of DKA treatment.
trap: Starting insulin without reviewing the potassium result.

stem: An adult with an acute stroke has a wet voice and coughs on saliva. No swallow assessment is recorded. What should the nurse do before offering oral intake?

stem: A nurse prevents a medicine reaching the wrong patient during identification checks. What is the best quality-improvement response?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove identification checks to reduce interruptions.

options.label: B
options.text: Review how the mismatch arose and improve the vulnerable process.

options.label: C
options.text: Close the matter because the final check worked.

options.label: D
options.text: Remind only the involved nurse to be more careful.

answerText: Review how the mismatch arose and improve the vulnerable process.
rationale: A successful interception can reveal an earlier process failure. Examining that process supports prevention beyond individual vigilance.

misconceptions.A: Removing a protective check increases risk.
misconceptions.C: The earlier failure could recur despite this successful check.
misconceptions.D: A reminder alone does not address the process weakness.

pearl: Near misses are opportunities to improve processes.
trap: Assuming no harm means no process problem.

stem: Two units have different numbers of patients with devices. Which measure is most useful for comparing their device-associated infection frequency?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of staff on duty when the first infection was detected.

options.label: B
options.text: Infections per 1,000 device-days using the same case definition.

options.label: C
options.text: The total number of infections without an exposure denominator.

options.label: D
options.text: The total number of all ward admissions regardless of device use.

answerText: Infections per 1,000 device-days using the same case definition.
rationale: Device-days measure relevant exposure time. A common case definition is also needed for a meaningful comparison.

misconceptions.A: Staffing at detection is not the exposure denominator.
misconceptions.C: Raw counts may reflect different exposure volumes.
misconceptions.D: All admissions do not measure time at risk from the device.

pearl: Compare rates using a relevant denominator and a consistent definition.
trap: Interpreting raw counts as comparable risk.

stem: A critical test result is given verbally during a busy shift. Which communication step is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Read back the patient identifiers and result, confirm them, and escalate promptly.

options.label: B
options.text: Write a brief number on scrap paper and confirm it after the shift.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the result to another patient’s nurse without identifiers.

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for the printed report before acknowledging the message.

answerText: Read back the patient identifiers and result, confirm them, and escalate promptly.
rationale: Read-back checks that the receiver heard the correct patient and result. Prompt escalation is still needed after confirmation.

misconceptions.B: Delayed confirmation can leave a transcription error uncorrected.
misconceptions.C: Missing identifiers creates a wrong-patient risk.
misconceptions.D: Waiting for paper can delay action on a critical result.

pearl: Confirm both patient and result during critical verbal communication.
trap: Treating a heard message as a confirmed message.
